fuentes/memoria-de-fontaneda/titulo.texto: Memoir of the Things, the Coast and the Indians of Florida

fuentes/memoria-de-fontaneda/soporte.texto: Manuscript, in the Archivo de Indias

fuentes/memoria-de-fontaneda/resumen.texto: Account by a Spaniard who lived seventeen years as a captive among the Calusa of southern Florida, after being shipwrecked as a boy around 1549. It describes the peoples and chiefs of the peninsula, the authority of the Calusa chief over dozens of towns that paid him tribute, their religion and the fate of the shipwrecked, many of whom were killed. Buckingham Smith translated it into English in 1854.

fuentes/memoria-de-fontaneda/por_que_imp.texto: It is almost the only description from within a complex society of fishers and gatherers without agriculture, before the missions; written by a captive, it mixes what was seen with what was heard.

fuentes/memoria-de-fontaneda/leer.0.titu.texto: Buckingham Smith’s English translation (Washington, 1854), together with a letter by Hernando de Soto, at Internet Archive

fuentes/history-of-the-american-indians-.texto: Book by a trader who lived for decades among the Chickasaws, Cherokees, Creeks, Choctaws and Catawbas. It describes their government, ceremonies, warfare, the torture of prisoners and trade with the English. The first half attempts to show, with supposed similarities of language and rite, that Indians descended from the lost tribes of Israel.
It is one of the richest sources on the Southeastern peoples in the 18th century; the Israelite thesis, which has no foundation, shows how Europeans sought to fit Indians into biblical history.

fuentes/viajes-de-bartram/titulo.texto: Travels Through North and South Carolina, Georgia, East and West Florida

fuentes/viajes-de-bartram/resumen.texto: Account of a naturalist’s journey through the Southeast between 1773 and 1777, with plants and animals and chapters on the Creeks, Cherokees and Seminoles: their towns, council houses, the green corn festival (busk) and their government. He also describes ancient mounds and plazas, such as those at Ocmulgee, which he attributes to earlier peoples.

fuentes/viajes-de-bartram/por_que_import.texto: It is a direct and generally favorable testimony of the Southeastern peoples before American expansion, much read by the Romantics.

fuentes/description-of-the-antiquities-a.texto: Description of the Antiquities Discovered in Ohio and Other Western States
Article in Archaeologia Americana, vol. 1, of the American Antiquarian Society

The first extensive description of Ohio’s earthworks, with plans of enclosures, mounds and roads, and the classification of antiquities into Indian, European and those of an earlier people. Atwater held that the larger works had been built by a people distinct from the Indians, who had arrived from Asia and later migrated toward Mexico.
Together with Squier and Davis’s work, it gave academic form to the myth of the “Mound Builders,” refuted in 1894.
Archaeologia Americana, vol. 1 (1820), at Internet Archive

fuentes/walam-olum-rafinesque/idioma_ori.texto: English, with an alleged text in Lenape

fuentes/walam-olum-rafinesque/soporte.texto: Published in The American Nations, vol. 1

fuentes/walam-olum-rafinesque/resumen.texto: A series of 183 pictograms with verses in Lenape and their translation, which Rafinesque presented as a chronicle of the Lenape from creation and a migration from Asia to their arrival in the east, copied from wooden tablets he said he had received in 1820. Nobody ever saw the tablets. David Oestreicher showed in 1994, using Rafinesque’s drafts, that the Lenape text had been translated from English and assembled from published vocabularies.

fuentes/walam-olum-rafinesque/por_que_im.texto: It was treated as an authentic document for more than a century and still circulates; it is an example of a fraud attributed to an Indigenous people.

fuentes/walam-olum-rafinesque/leer.0.tit.texto: The American Nations, vol. 1 (1836), at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/ancient-monuments-squier-davis/t.texto: Ancient Monuments of the Mississippi Valley

fuentes/ancient-monuments-squier-davis/s.texto: Book, first volume of the Smithsonian Contributions to Knowledge

fuentes/ancient-monuments-squier-davis/r.texto: Survey by E. G. Squier and Edwin H. Davis, made between 1845 and 1847, of some two hundred sites with plans of geometric enclosures, mounds and effigies, among them Newark, Mound City and the Serpent Mound. It classifies the works by function (defensive works, sacred enclosures, sacrificial and burial mounds) and concludes that they were built by a vanished people, distinct from the known Indians.

fuentes/ancient-monuments-squier-davis/p.texto: Many of the sites he drew were later razed by the plow and by cities, and his plans are sometimes the only record; his conclusion fed the myth of the “Mound Builders.”

fuentes/ancient-monuments-squier-davis/l.texto: Full text with plates at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/league-of-the-iroquois/resumen.texto: Description of the League of the Six Nations, written with information from the Seneca Ely S. Parker, to whom it is dedicated: the Grand Council of fifty chiefs, the clans and the election of chiefs by clan mothers, religion, festivals, language and material life. It presents the League as a federation with its own political constitution.

fuentes/league-of-the-iroquois/por_que_i.texto: It is considered the first scientific ethnography of an Indigenous people and was the basis of Morgan’s kinship studies; it describes the League in the mid-19th century, after two centuries of contact.

fuentes/ancient-society-morgan/resumen.texto: Theory of social evolution in stages of “savagery,” “barbarism” and “civilization,” defined by inventions such as pottery, the bow or writing, and of the evolution of the family and of property. It uses the Iroquois as a model of clan organization, placing them in “lower barbarism,” and compares them with the Greeks and Romans.

fuentes/ancient-society-morgan/por_que_i.texto: Engels relied on it for The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State (1884); later anthropology abandoned its evolutionary scheme and its stages.

fuentes/cuenta-de-inviernos-de-lone-dog/.texto: Pictographic calendar of the Yanktonai, a branch of the Dakota, with one drawing for each winter from 1800 to 1871, recalling the event that gave the year its name: smallpox and measles epidemics, wars and peace with other peoples, stolen horses, a meteor shower (1833). Army officer Garrick Mallery published it in 1877 and in the 1886 report of the Bureau of Ethnology.
It is an example of the history kept by the Plains peoples themselves, comparable with written documents and astronomical dates.
Pictographs of the North American Indians, by Garrick Mallery (1886), with Lone Dog’s count, at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/cartas-de-catlin/titulo.texto: Letters and Notes on the Manners, Customs, and Condition of the North American Indians

fuentes/cartas-de-catlin/resumen.texto: Letters from the painter about his travels across the plains and the upper Missouri between 1830 and 1836, with more than three hundred engravings. He describes the Mandans, their villages of earth lodges and the okipa ceremony, with its trials of pain, and the Lakotas, Blackfeet, Crows and other peoples.

fuentes/cartas-de-catlin/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main testimony about the Mandans before the smallpox epidemic of 1837 reduced them to little more than a hundred people; Catlin called for a large national park where Indians could continue their way of life.

fuentes/cartas-de-catlin/leer.0.titulo.texto: Volume 1 of the 1857 edition (Illustrations of the Manners, Customs, and Condition of the North American Indians) at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/cliff-dwellers-of-the-mesa-verde.texto: The Cliff Dwellers of the Mesa Verde

Report on the 1891 excavations at Mesa Verde, with plans, photographs and descriptions of the pottery, textiles, tools and burials of the cliff houses. It relates these ruins to the living pueblos of New Mexico and Arizona.
It is the first systematic study of Mesa Verde; the export of its collection to Europe was one of the reasons for the 1906 antiquities act.
Original edition (Stockholm and Chicago, 1893) at Internet Archive

fuentes/kwakiutl-boas-1897/titulo.texto: The Social Organization and the Secret Societies of the Kwakiutl Indians

fuentes/kwakiutl-boas-1897/soporte.texto: Report of the United States National Museum for 1895

fuentes/kwakiutl-boas-1897/resumen.texto: Study by Franz Boas, made with texts by George Hunt, on lineages (numaym), ranks, the potlatch as a way of validating titles and distributing goods, copper as an object of prestige, and the winter ceremonies of the secret societies, among them the hamat’sa or “cannibal dancer.”

fuentes/kwakiutl-boas-1897/por_que_impor.texto: It is the classic description of the potlatch, written when Canada had already banned it; much of what is repeated about it comes from here.

fuentes/code-of-handsome-lake/titulo.texto: The Code of Handsome Lake, the Seneca Prophet

fuentes/code-of-handsome-lake/soporte.texto: Bulletin of the New York State Museum

fuentes/code-of-handsome-lake/resumen.texto: Version of the Gaiwiio, the “good message” of Handsome Lake, recited by the preacher Edward Cornplanter and translated by Parker, with notes on the ceremonies of the Longhouse. It contains prohibitions on alcohol, witchcraft and abortion, and rules on family and work.

fuentes/code-of-handsome-lake/por_que_im.texto: It is the written basis of the Longhouse religion, one of the Indigenous religious responses to the crisis that followed the American Revolution.

fuentes/gran-ley-de-la-paz/titulo.texto: The Constitution of the Five Nations (the Great Law of Peace)

fuentes/gran-ley-de-la-paz/idioma_origin.texto: English, translated from Mohawk and other Iroquoian languages

fuentes/gran-ley-de-la-paz/soporte.texto: Bulletin of the New York State Museum (1916)

fuentes/gran-ley-de-la-paz/resumen.texto: Arthur C. Parker’s edition of two written versions of the Great Law of Peace (Kayanerenkó:wa), the League’s oral constitution: that of Seth Newhouse, compiled between the 1880s and 1910, and the one prepared in 1900 by a committee of chiefs of the Six Nations of the Grand River. It contains the account of Deganawida and Hiawatha, the list of the fifty chiefs’ titles, the role of the clan mothers, the procedures of the Grand Council and the mourning rites.

fuentes/gran-ley-de-la-paz/por_que_impor.texto: It is the most cited written version of the Great Law; since it was fixed in writing almost four centuries after the founding it narrates, it cannot by itself be used to date that founding.

fuentes/song-of-hiawatha/resumen.texto: Poem telling the life of Hiawatha, an Ojibwe hero on the shore of Lake Superior, his love for Minnehaha and his farewell when the white missionaries arrive. Longfellow took the accounts from Henry Schoolcraft, who confused the Iroquois Hiawatha with the Ojibwe hero Manabozho.

fuentes/song-of-hiawatha/por_que_importa.texto: It was an enormous success and fixed in the public mind the confusion between the founder of the Iroquois League and a figure from Ojibwe myth; it also spread the romantic image of the vanishing Indian.

fuentes/ley-de-antiguedades-de-1906/titu.texto: An Act for the Preservation of American Antiquities (Antiquities Act)

fuentes/ley-de-antiguedades-de-1906/resu.texto: Law that penalizes excavating or destroying ancient ruins and objects on federal lands without permission, requires that excavations be carried out by scientific institutions, and authorizes the president to declare national monuments. Among the first were Montezuma Castle (1906) and Chaco Canyon (1907).

fuentes/ley-de-antiguedades-de-1906/por_.texto: It arose from alarm over the looting of Southwestern sites such as Mesa Verde and Chaco, and it marks the beginning of the protection of archaeological heritage in the United States.

fuentes/ley-de-antiguedades-de-1906/leer.texto: Text and background on the National Park Service website

fuentes/ley-nagpra/titulo.texto: Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA)

fuentes/ley-nagpra/resumen.texto: Law that requires museums and agencies receiving federal funds to inventory human remains and funerary and sacred objects of Indigenous origin and to return them to tribes that demonstrate cultural affiliation, and that protects graves found on federal and tribal lands.

fuentes/ley-nagpra/por_que_importa.texto: It changed the relationship between archaeology and Indigenous peoples; its critics point out that it can block studies of very old remains, as the Kennewick Man case showed.

fuentes/ley-nagpra/leer.0.titulo.texto: Current text in the United States Code (Cornell Legal Information Institute)

fuentes/prohibicion-del-potlatch-1884/ti.texto: 1884 Amendment to the Indian Act (ban on the potlatch)

fuentes/prohibicion-del-potlatch-1884/so.texto: Act of the Parliament of Canada

fuentes/prohibicion-del-potlatch-1884/re.texto: Amendment that made it a crime, from January 1, 1885, to hold the potlatch or the tamanawas dance of Pacific Coast peoples, punishable by imprisonment. It was reinforced in 1895 and 1918 and was removed in the 1951 revision of the Indian Act.

fuentes/prohibicion-del-potlatch-1884/po.texto: It is the document of Canada’s policy of suppressing Indigenous ceremonies; missionaries and officials justified it by the expense and destruction of goods at the feasts.

fuentes/report-on-the-mound-explorations.texto: Report on the Mound Explorations of the Bureau of Ethnology
Twelfth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology (730 pages)

Result of the mound survey that the Bureau of Ethnology carried out between 1881 and 1890 at thousands of sites in the eastern United States. It shows that the objects, techniques and burial customs of the mounds match those of known Indigenous peoples, that some mounds were still in use when Europeans arrived, and that the Cherokees and other peoples had built them.
It dismantled with data the myth of a lost race of “Mound Builders”; it is one of the first major field archaeology projects organized by a state.
Twelfth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology (1894) at Internet Archive

fuentes/handbook-of-north-american-india.texto: Smithsonian collective work; 15 of the 20 planned volumes were published

Encyclopedia in volumes by cultural area (Arctic, Subarctic, Northeast, Southeast, Plains, Southwest, Great Basin, Plateau, California, Northwest Coast) and by topic (relations with whites, languages, population), written by hundreds of specialists. Each people has a chapter on its history, language, organization and population.
It is the reference work on the Indigenous peoples of North America and the basis of the division into cultural areas.

fuentes/thornton-1987/resumen.texto: Demographic history of the Indigenous peoples of the United States and Canada. Thornton estimates more than 5 million people in the continental territory of the United States and more than 7 million north of Mexico around 1492, and a decline to some 250,000 in the United States around 1900, due to epidemics, wars, forced removals and the destruction of ways of life. He uses the word “holocaust” for the process as a whole.

fuentes/thornton-1987/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most cited synthesis of the high estimates; its starting figures are above those of Ubelaker and below those of Dobyns.

fuentes/ubelaker-1988/titulo.texto: The Population of the Indians of North America from 1500 to 1985

fuentes/ubelaker-1988/soporte.texto: Article in American Journal of Physical Anthropology 77

fuentes/ubelaker-1988/resumen.texto: Estimate of the Indigenous population north of Mexico around 1500, adding up the figures of specialists for each cultural area in the Handbook of North American Indians: about 1.9 million people. It follows the decline to a low around 1900 and the recovery in the 20th century.

fuentes/ubelaker-1988/por_que_importa.texto: It represents moderate estimates, built region by region; it shows the gap between the figures (from 1 to 18 million) debated for the same territory.

fuentes/fenn-2001/titulo.texto: Pox Americana: The Great Smallpox Epidemic of 1775-1782

fuentes/fenn-2001/resumen.texto: History of the smallpox epidemic that spread across North America during the American Revolution, from Boston and Mexico to the plains, Hudson Bay and the Pacific coast. It reconstructs its routes through trade and war and estimates that it killed more than 130,000 people, largely Indigenous.

fuentes/fenn-2001/por_que_importa.texto: It shows that many epidemics reached inland peoples before Europeans did, through Indigenous trade networks, and that the contagion did not require intent.

fuentes/donald-1997/titulo.texto: Aboriginal Slavery on the Northwest Coast of North America

fuentes/donald-1997/resumen.texto: Study of the testimony of travelers, traders, missionaries and ethnographers on slavery among the peoples from Alaska to California. It concludes that slave status was hereditary, that slaves were obtained through war and trade, were bought and sold, and were sometimes killed in ceremonies or given away at the potlatch, and that they were an important part of the population and of the labor in many groups.

fuentes/donald-1997/por_que_importa.texto: It is the reference work that established that slavery was a central, not marginal, institution of those societies before the arrival of Europeans.

fuentes/ames-maschner-1999/titulo.texto: Peoples of the Northwest Coast: Their Archaeology and Prehistory

fuentes/ames-maschner-1999/autor.texto: Kenneth M. Ames and Herbert D. G. Maschner

fuentes/ames-maschner-1999/resumen.texto: Synthesis of ten thousand years of Pacific coast archaeology, from Alaska to northern California: salmon fishing, plank houses, hereditary ranks, warfare, fortifications and slavery. It shows how complex and unequal societies emerged among fishers and gatherers without agriculture.

fuentes/ames-maschner-1999/por_que_impor.texto: It refutes the idea that inequality and organized warfare arrived only with agriculture.

fuentes/pauketat-2009/titulo.texto: Cahokia: Ancient America’s Great City on the Mississippi

fuentes/pauketat-2009/resumen.texto: History of Cahokia based on excavations: the “big bang” around 1050, when the city was rebuilt according to a plan, Monks Mound was raised and immigrants arrived from the region; Mound 72 and its sacrifices; the spread of its influence along the Mississippi and its decline after 1200.

fuentes/pauketat-2009/por_que_importa.texto: It defends reading Cahokia as a city and a powerful political center; other archaeologists see it as a smaller chiefdom.

fuentes/fowler-1999-monticulo-72/titulo.texto: The Mound 72 Area: A Dedicated and Sacred Space in Early Cahokia

fuentes/fowler-1999-monticulo-72/soporte.texto: Report of the Illinois State Museum (with J. Rose, B. Vander Leest and S. Ahler)

fuentes/fowler-1999-monticulo-72/resumen.texto: Final report of the 1967-1971 excavations at Mound 72: a ring of posts and, above it, about 270 individuals in burials and pits, among them the “bead burial” with about 20,000 shell beads, pits with dozens of young women, and a group of four men without heads or hands, interpreted as eleventh-century sacrifices.

fuentes/fowler-1999-monticulo-72/por_que.texto: It is the main evidence of mass human sacrifice in Mississippian culture.

fuentes/emerson-2016-monticulo-72/titulo.texto: Lost Paradigms: Reinterpreting the Bead Burial of Cahokia’s Mound 72

fuentes/emerson-2016-monticulo-72/autor.texto: Thomas E. Emerson, Kristin M. Hedman and others

fuentes/emerson-2016-monticulo-72/resume.texto: New analysis of the bones of the central burial of Mound 72: among the bodies associated with the bed of beads there are women, and not only men. The authors propose that the scene represents pairs of men and women linked to fertility and cosmology, and not a single warrior chief with his retinue.

fuentes/emerson-2016-monticulo-72/por_qu.texto: It shows how the interpretation of a find changed when the data were reviewed; it does not dispute that sacrifices took place.

fuentes/saunders-1997/titulo.texto: A Mound Complex in Louisiana at 5400-5000 Years Ago

fuentes/saunders-1997/resumen.texto: Presents the radiocarbon dates and stratigraphy of Watson Brake, a ring of eleven mounds joined by embankments in northern Louisiana, built by hunters, fishers and gatherers about 5,400 to 5,000 years ago.

fuentes/saunders-1997/por_que_importa.texto: It showed that monumental architecture in North America began millennia before agriculture and chiefdoms.

fuentes/willey-emerson-1993/titulo.texto: Osteology and Archaeology of the Crow Creek Massacre

fuentes/willey-emerson-1993/autor.texto: P. Willey and Thomas E. Emerson

fuentes/willey-emerson-1993/soporte.texto: Article in Plains Anthropologist 38; expands on Willey’s book Prehistoric Warfare on the Great Plains (1990)

fuentes/willey-emerson-1993/resumen.texto: Analysis of the remains of at least 486 people found in the fortification ditch of a village on the South Dakota plains, killed in a single attack at the beginning of the 14th century. Nearly all the skulls show scalping marks and many bodies were mutilated; the skeletons show malnutrition and earlier wounds.

fuentes/willey-emerson-1993/por_que_impo.texto: It is the clearest evidence of a mass killing among Indigenous peoples before contact.

fuentes/milner-1991/titulo.texto: Warfare in Late Prehistoric West-Central Illinois

fuentes/milner-1991/autor.texto: George R. Milner, Eve Anderson and Virginia G. Smith

fuentes/milner-1991/resumen.texto: Study of the Norris Farms 36 cemetery, of the Oneota culture, with 264 individuals: about a third of the adults died violently, with arrow and mace wounds, scalping and decapitation, and many bodies were left exposed for a time before burial.

fuentes/milner-1991/por_que_importa.texto: It shows endemic warfare, of ambushes and small but continuous attacks, that killed a huge part of an agricultural community.

fuentes/man-corn/titulo.texto: Man Corn: Cannibalism and Violence in the Prehistoric American Southwest

fuentes/man-corn/resumen.texto: Review of dozens of assemblages of human bones in the Southwest with cut marks, burning, fractures to extract marrow and “pot polish,” which the authors consider evidence of cannibalism, concentrated between 900 and 1300 around Chaco. They propose that it was introduced by groups who came from Mexico as a form of terror and social control; the title translates the Nahuatl word tlacatlaolli.

fuentes/man-corn/por_que_importa.texto: It made the strongest case of anyone for cannibalism among the ancestral Puebloans; its hypothesis of a Mexican origin is the most disputed part.

fuentes/billman-2000/titulo.texto: Cannibalism, Warfare, and Drought in the Mesa Verde Region During the Twelfth Century A.D.

fuentes/billman-2000/autor.texto: Brian R. Billman, Patricia M. Lambert and Banks L. Leonard

fuentes/billman-2000/resumen.texto: Study of Cowboy Wash and other sites in the Mesa Verde region where, around 1150, remains of people who had been dismembered, cooked and broken were found. The authors link these episodes to drought and the collapse of the Chaco system, and interpret them as violence between communities that included cannibalism.

fuentes/billman-2000/por_que_importa.texto: It is the archaeological report on the most famous case in the debate.

fuentes/marlar-2000/titulo.texto: Biochemical Evidence of Cannibalism at a Prehistoric Puebloan Site in Southwestern Colorado

fuentes/marlar-2000/resumen.texto: Reports that human myoglobin, a muscle protein, was detected in a coprolite found in the hearth of a house at Cowboy Wash, something that could only be there if a person had eaten human flesh; human protein remains were also found in a pot and in stone tools.

fuentes/marlar-2000/por_que_importa.texto: It was presented as the first direct proof of human flesh consumption in the Southwest; the specificity of the test and its interpretation were disputed.

fuentes/marlar-2000/leer.0.titulo.texto: Abstract and article on the Nature website

fuentes/dongoske-2000/titulo.texto: A Critique of the Cannibalism Claim at Cowboy Wash

fuentes/dongoske-2000/autor.texto: Kurt E. Dongoske, Debra L. Martin and T. J. Ferguson

fuentes/dongoske-2000/resumen.texto: Response by an archaeologist from the Hopi cultural preservation office, a bioarchaeologist and an anthropologist who works with the Zuni: they argue that the processed bones prove extreme violence but not necessarily cannibalism, that there are other explanations, such as the execution and destruction of the body of alleged witches, and that the word “cannibalism” was used carelessly and harmed descendant peoples.

fuentes/dongoske-2000/por_que_importa.texto: It summarizes the main critique of the cannibalism thesis and the position of the Hopi and Zuni peoples.

fuentes/kuckelman-2002/titulo.texto: Bioarchaeology and Taphonomy of Violence at Castle Rock and Sand Canyon

fuentes/kuckelman-2002/autor.texto: Kristin A. Kuckelman, Ricky R. Lightfoot and Debra L. Martin

fuentes/kuckelman-2002/resumen.texto: Study of the remains of two villages in the McElmo Canyon, near Mesa Verde, attacked around 1280, in the midst of drought. At Castle Rock at least 41 people of all ages were found, killed with blows to the head and wounds, several with processing marks; the village was abandoned after the attack.

fuentes/kuckelman-2002/por_que_importa.texto: It documents the violence that accompanied the abandonment of the Mesa Verde region at the end of the 13th century.

fuentes/potter-chuipka-2010/titulo.texto: Mutilation of Human Remains at an Early Southwestern Village: Evidence for Ethnic Violence

fuentes/potter-chuipka-2010/autor.texto: James M. Potter and Jason P. Chuipka

fuentes/potter-chuipka-2010/soporte.texto: Article in Journal of Anthropological Archaeology 29

fuentes/potter-chuipka-2010/resumen.texto: Analyzes the remains of about 35 people from Sacred Ridge, a village from around 800 near Durango, Colorado, who were struck, dismembered and burned. Based on differences in the bones and in the architecture, the authors propose that the victims belonged to a different group from the attackers.

fuentes/potter-chuipka-2010/por_que_impo.texto: It pushes organized violence in the Southwest back to the 9th century, well before Chaco.

fuentes/turner-morris-1970/soporte.texto: Article in American Antiquity 35, with Nancy T. Morris

fuentes/turner-morris-1970/resumen.texto: Study of a pit with about thirty people of different ages, found in 1964 at Polacca Wash, on Hopi land, with cut, broken and burned bones. The authors link it to Hopi oral tradition about the destruction of Awatovi in 1700, according to which the captives were killed and dismembered on the way.

fuentes/turner-morris-1970/por_que_impor.texto: It combines archaeology and oral tradition in a case of violence between Indigenous peoples already in the colonial period.

fuentes/kennett-2017/titulo.texto: Archaeogenomic Evidence for a Prehistoric Matrilineal Dynasty

fuentes/kennett-2017/resumen.texto: Sequences the mitochondrial DNA of nine people buried in Room 33 of Pueblo Bonito, Chaco’s richest crypt, and dates their bones: all share the same maternal lineage for about 330 years, from around 800 to 1130.

fuentes/kennett-2017/por_que_importa.texto: It is the strongest evidence that a hereditary elite through the maternal line governed Chaco; the study was criticized for not having consulted descendant peoples.

fuentes/douglass-1929/titulo.texto: The Secret of the Southwest Solved by Talkative Tree-Rings

fuentes/douglass-1929/resumen.texto: Tells how a charred beam found at Show Low, Arizona, the HH-39, linked the tree-ring chronology of living trees with that of the beams in the ruins, and for the first time gives exact years for Pueblo Bonito, Mesa Verde, Aztec and other sites.

fuentes/douglass-1929/por_que_importa.texto: It made Southwestern archaeology the best-dated in the world and revealed the great drought of the late 13th century.

fuentes/mann-fields-1997/titulo.texto: A Sign in the Sky: The Date of the Haudenosaunee League

fuentes/mann-fields-1997/autor.texto: Barbara A. Mann and Jerry L. Fields

fuentes/mann-fields-1997/soporte.texto: Article in American Indian Culture and Research Journal 21

fuentes/mann-fields-1997/resumen.texto: Proposes that the League was founded in 1142, identifying with the total solar eclipse of August 31 of that year the darkening of the sky that, according to tradition, decided the Senecas to join. It relies on the chronology of oral tradition and on calculations of the eclipses visible in the region.

fuentes/mann-fields-1997/por_que_importa.texto: It is the earliest proposed date; most archaeologists reject it because it does not fit the sequence of Iroquoian villages.

fuentes/snow-1994/resumen.texto: History of the Iroquois from their archaeological origins to the present, based on the sequence of Mohawk and other nations’ villages: the growth and fortification of villages, the arrival of epidemics and European trade, and the history of the League. It places the formation of the League around 1525.

fuentes/snow-1994/por_que_importa.texto: It represents the late date for the League, supported by archaeology.

fuentes/fenton-1998/titulo.texto: The Great Law and the Longhouse: A Political History of the Iroquois Confederacy

fuentes/fenton-1998/resumen.texto: History of the League from its founding according to tradition to the 18th century, with the workings of the Grand Council, the condolence rites and diplomacy with the Dutch, French and English, based on treaty records and decades of work with the Haudenosaunee themselves.

fuentes/fenton-1998/por_que_importa.texto: It is the major work of 20th-century Iroquois studies.

fuentes/tooker-1988/titulo.texto: The United States Constitution and the Iroquois League

fuentes/tooker-1988/resumen.texto: Reviews the documents of the 1787 convention and the writings of its drafters and concludes that there is no evidence that the Iroquois League served as a model for the United States Constitution. She points out that the League rested on the consensus of chiefs chosen by the clan mothers, very different from a representative federal government.

fuentes/tooker-1988/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main critique of the thesis of Iroquois influence.

fuentes/exemplar-of-liberty/titulo.texto: Exemplar of Liberty: Native America and the Evolution of Democracy

fuentes/exemplar-of-liberty/autor.texto: Donald A. Grinde and Bruce E. Johansen

fuentes/exemplar-of-liberty/soporte.texto: Book, from the UCLA American Indian Studies Center

fuentes/exemplar-of-liberty/resumen.texto: Argues that the institutions of the Iroquois League and of other peoples influenced the colonists’ political ideas and the formation of the United States, citing Canassatego’s speech at Lancaster (1744), which advised the colonies to unite, Franklin’s Albany Plan (1754) and writings by Jefferson and others.

fuentes/exemplar-of-liberty/por_que_impo.texto: It is the main exposition of the thesis of Iroquois influence, which Congress recognized in a 1988 resolution and which most historians consider exaggerated.

fuentes/gehring-starna-1987/titulo.texto: The Tawagonshi Treaty of 1613: The Final Chapter

fuentes/gehring-starna-1987/autor.texto: Charles T. Gehring, William A. Starna and William N. Fenton

fuentes/gehring-starna-1987/resumen.texto: Analyzes the Dutch-language document presented as the text of the 1613 treaty between the Mohawks and the Dutch and shows, from its language, spelling, names and dates, that it is a modern forgery.

fuentes/gehring-starna-1987/por_que_impo.texto: It separates the false document from the Haudenosaunee tradition of the Two Row Wampum, which does not depend on that paper.

fuentes/wallace-1970/titulo.texto: The Death and Rebirth of the Seneca

fuentes/wallace-1970/resumen.texto: History of the Senecas from their power in the 18th century to the crisis that followed the American Revolution, with the loss of land, alcoholism and reservation life, and of the religious movement of Handsome Lake, with its reforms and witch hunts, as a “revitalization.”

fuentes/wallace-1970/por_que_importa.texto: It is the classic study of an Indigenous religious movement and of how a society rebuilt itself after defeat.

fuentes/oestreicher-1994/titulo.texto: Unmasking the Walam Olum: A Nineteenth-Century Fraud

fuentes/oestreicher-1994/soporte.texto: Article in Bulletin of the Archaeological Society of New Jersey 49

fuentes/oestreicher-1994/resumen.texto: Through a study of Rafinesque’s manuscripts, shows that the Lenape text of the Walam Olum has corrections typical of someone translating from English, words taken from published vocabularies, and errors that a native speaker would not make.

fuentes/oestreicher-1994/por_que_importa.texto: It closed a debate of more than a century over the authenticity of the document.

fuentes/mainfort-kwas-2004/titulo.texto: The Bat Creek Stone Revisited: A Fraud Exposed

fuentes/mainfort-kwas-2004/autor.texto: Robert C. Mainfort and Mary L. Kwas

fuentes/mainfort-kwas-2004/resumen.texto: Shows that the inscription on the Bat Creek stone, presented since 1971 as ancient Hebrew, copies an illustration from a Masonic book published in 1870, and that the 1889 discovery has inconsistencies that point to the excavator.

fuentes/mainfort-kwas-2004/por_que_impor.texto: It refutes the main “proof” of a Hebrew contact with America.

fuentes/satake-1996/titulo.texto: Date and Magnitude of a Great Cascadia Earthquake from Japanese Records of the January 1700 Tsunami

fuentes/satake-1996/autor.texto: Kenji Satake, Kunihiko Shimazaki, Yoshinobu Tsuji and Kazue Ueda

fuentes/satake-1996/resumen.texto: Based on Japanese documents recording a tsunami with no local earthquake on January 27 and 28, 1700, calculates that it was produced by an earthquake of magnitude close to 9 on the Cascadia subduction zone, around nine o’clock at night on January 26, 1700.

fuentes/satake-1996/por_que_importa.texto: It gave the exact date of an earthquake that was known only from geology and from Indigenous oral traditions.

fuentes/satake-1996/leer.0.titulo.texto: Abstract and article on the Nature website

fuentes/atwater-2005/soporte.texto: Professional Paper 1707 of the United States Geological Survey

fuentes/atwater-2005/resumen.texto: Brings together the Japanese documents on the 1700 tsunami, the geology of the Washington and Oregon coast (sunken soils, tsunami sand, dead cedars dated by their rings) and the oral traditions of coastal peoples about a great shaking and flood.

fuentes/atwater-2005/por_que_importa.texto: It is an example of how Indigenous oral tradition, written records from another continent and geology converge on a single event.

fuentes/atwater-2005/leer.0.titulo.texto: Full report on the United States Geological Survey website

fuentes/hamalainen-2008/resumen.texto: Argues that between 1750 and 1850 the Comanches built a hegemonic power on the southern plains, based on the horse, the bison, trade, tribute and the capture of people, which dominated neighboring Indigenous peoples and the colonies of Spain and Mexico and later Texas. It uses Spanish, Mexican and American documents.

fuentes/hamalainen-2008/por_que_importa.texto: It won the Bancroft Prize; its critics dispute whether “empire” describes a society without a state or a center, but not the facts of domination and slavery that it documents.

fuentes/a-new-voyage-to-carolina/resumen.texto: A description of the geography, natural history and Indigenous peoples of the Carolinas, with the journal of his 1700–1701 journey through the interior, which its title presents as “a thousand miles” travelled among several nations of Indians, with their customs and manners. It went through several editions, including German and French translations, and its circulation drew settlers to North Carolina.

fuentes/a-new-voyage-to-carolina/por_que.texto: It is one of the most complete colonial reports on the Indigenous peoples of the Carolinas at the beginning of the eighteenth century. Its author was killed by the Tuscarora, one of the peoples he describes.

personas/deganawida/resumen.texto: Founder of the Haudenosaunee League according to Iroquois oral tradition: a prophet born among the Wendat who crossed Lake Ontario and convinced five feuding nations to accept the Great Law of Peace. His story is known from oral versions put in writing since the 19th century; there is no documentary proof of his existence or of his date, which according to the authors ranges from the 12th to the 16th century.

personas/hiawatha/resumen.texto: Co-founder of the Iroquois League according to tradition: an Onondaga or Mohawk chief who, after losing his daughters, joined Deganawida and carried his message from nation to nation; tradition credits him with the use of wampum as a mourning token and as a record. He has no relation to the hero of Longfellow’s poem (1855), which took the name but told Ojibwe legends.

personas/tadodaho/resumen.texto: Onondaga chief who, according to Iroquois tradition, opposed the peace of Deganawida and Hiawatha and was depicted with snakes in his hair. When he accepted the League, his name became the title of the Onondaga chief who convenes the Grand Council, which still exists.

personas/handsome-lake/resumen.texto: Seneca, half-brother of the chief Cornplanter, who in 1799, sick and an alcoholic, had visions and began preaching the Gaiwiio (“good message”): give up alcohol and witchcraft, care for the family, and have men cultivate the land. His preaching gave rise to the Longhouse religion, still practiced among the Haudenosaunee; it also promoted witchcraft accusations that ended in executions, as documented by Anthony F. C. Wallace.

personas/serpiente-tatuada/resumen.texto: War chief of the Natchez, brother of the Great Sun and ally of the French. His funeral, in 1725, was described by his friend Le Page du Pratz: his wives and several servants were strangled to accompany him, according to a custom of the Natchez ruling lineages.

personas/hernando-de-escalante-fontaneda.texto: Son of Spaniards from Cartagena de Indias who was shipwrecked as a boy on the Florida coast around 1549 and lived seventeen years as a captive among the Calusa, until Pedro Menéndez de Avilés rescued him in 1566. His Memoir, written around 1575, describes the peoples of southern Florida and the power of the Calusa chief.

personas/james-adair/resumen.texto: Irish trader who for decades dealt with the Chickasaws, Cherokees and other Southeastern peoples and published The History of the American Indians in 1775. The book is a valuable source on the life, warfare and trade of those peoples, but it is built to prove that Indians descended from the lost tribes of Israel, a thesis with no basis.

personas/william-bartram/resumen.texto: Naturalist from Philadelphia who traveled through the Carolinas, Georgia and Florida between 1773 and 1777 and published his Travels in 1791, with descriptions of the Creek, Cherokee and Seminole peoples, their towns, and ancient mounds such as those at Ocmulgee.

personas/george-catlin/resumen.texto: Painter from Pennsylvania who between 1830 and 1836 traveled through the plains and the upper Missouri and portrayed hundreds of Indigenous people from dozens of nations. His letters (1841) and his paintings of the Mandan okipa ceremony, painted in 1832, are a unique record of that people before the smallpox epidemic of 1837, although some of his contemporaries disputed details of his descriptions.

personas/henry-schoolcraft/resumen.texto: Indian agent at Sault Ste. Marie, married to the Ojibwe writer Jane Johnston, who published Ojibwe stories in Algic Researches (1839). He identified the Ojibwe hero Manabozho with the Iroquois Hiawatha, a confusion that Longfellow carried into The Song of Hiawatha (1855).

personas/caleb-atwater/resumen.texto: Lawyer and antiquarian from Circleville, Ohio, who published in 1820, in the journal of the American Antiquarian Society, the first extensive description of Ohio’s earthworks. He attributed the mounds to a people distinct from the Indians of his time, who had come from Asia and later migrated to Mexico, one of the foundations of the myth of the “Mound Builders.”

personas/constantine-rafinesque/resumen.texto: Naturalist born in Constantinople, author of thousands of plant and animal names, who published the Walam Olum, an alleged pictographic chronicle of the Lenape, in The American Nations (1836). The study of his manuscripts in the 1980s and 1990s showed that he himself had composed the text.

personas/ephraim-george-squier/resumen.texto: Journalist from Chillicothe, Ohio, who with Edwin H. Davis surveyed hundreds of mounds and earthen enclosures and published Ancient Monuments of the Mississippi Valley (1848), the first volume of the Smithsonian. He later served as a diplomat in Central America and studied the ruins of Peru.

personas/edwin-hamilton-davis/resumen.texto: Physician from Chillicothe, co-author with Squier of Ancient Monuments of the Mississippi Valley (1848). He assembled a large collection of objects from the Ohio mounds that ended up in England and is now in the British Museum.

personas/lewis-henry-morgan/resumen.texto: Lawyer from Rochester, New York, who, with the help of the Seneca Ely S. Parker, wrote League of the Iroquois (1851), considered the first scientific ethnography of an Indigenous people. His kinship studies (1871) and Ancient Society (1877), with its scheme of stages of “savagery,” “barbarism” and “civilization,” influenced Engels; later anthropology, from Boas on, abandoned that scheme.

personas/ely-s-parker/resumen.texto: Seneca from Tonawanda and chief of the League with the title Donehogawa, Morgan’s main informant and collaborator. He was an engineer, military secretary to Ulysses S. Grant during the Civil War, the one who wrote out the terms of the surrender at Appomattox (1865), and the first Native American to head the United States Office of Indian Affairs (1869–1871).

personas/arthur-c-parker/resumen.texto: Archaeologist at the New York State Museum, of Seneca descent and grandnephew of Ely S. Parker. He published The Code of Handsome Lake (1913) and The Constitution of the Five Nations (1916), with the written versions of the Iroquois Great Law.

personas/j-n-b-hewitt/resumen.texto: Ethnologist of Tuscarora descent who worked for half a century at the Smithsonian’s Bureau of American Ethnology, collecting and translating Iroquoian texts in their languages, among them versions of the founding of the League.

personas/john-wesley-powell/resumen.texto: Geologist and Civil War veteran who explored the Grand Canyon in 1869 and from 1879 directed the Smithsonian’s Bureau of Ethnology. He promoted the first classification of the Indigenous language families north of Mexico (1891) and Cyrus Thomas’s mound survey.

personas/cyrus-thomas/resumen.texto: Entomologist who from 1882 directed the mound exploration division of the Bureau of Ethnology. His 1894 report, based on thousands of sites, concluded that the mounds had been built by the ancestors of Indigenous peoples, against the idea of a lost race that he himself had once accepted.

personas/franz-boas/resumen.texto: German-born anthropologist based in New York, founder of cultural anthropology in the United States. From 1886 he studied the peoples of the Northwest Coast, above all the Kwakwaka’wakw, using texts in Indigenous languages gathered by George Hunt, and he rejected the evolutionary stage schemes and racial hierarchies of his time.

personas/george-hunt/resumen.texto: Son of an English trader and a Tlingit woman, raised at Fort Rupert among the Kwakwaka’wakw, he was for forty years Boas’s main collaborator: he wrote thousands of pages of texts in Kwak’wala, assembled collections and took part in ceremonies. He is co-author of much of what is known about 19th-century Kwakwaka’wakw society.

personas/richard-wetherill/resumen.texto: Rancher from Mancos, Colorado, who in December 1888, with his brother-in-law Charlie Mason, reached Cliff Palace and other cliff houses of Mesa Verde, which he excavated and whose objects he sold, and who spread the Navajo name “Anasazi.” He excavated Pueblo Bonito for the Hyde Exploring Expedition between 1896 and 1900; a Navajo killed him in 1910 after a dispute.

personas/gustaf-nordenskiold/resumen.texto: Swedish naturalist, son of the explorer Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld, who in 1891 excavated the Mesa Verde houses with the Wetherills more methodically than his contemporaries and published The Cliff Dwellers of the Mesa Verde (1893). He was briefly detained for shipping hundreds of objects to Europe; the collection ended up in the National Museum of Finland, which in 2020 returned the human remains and funerary objects to Indigenous peoples.

personas/a-e-douglass/resumen.texto: Astronomer at the University of Arizona who was looking for solar cycles in tree rings and created dendrochronology. In 1929, with a beam found at Show Low, he linked his ring sequence with that of the ruins and gave exact dates to Pueblo Bonito, Mesa Verde and other Southwestern sites; he also identified the great drought of 1276–1299.

personas/emil-haury/resumen.texto: Archaeologist at the University of Arizona who excavated Snaketown in 1934–1935 and in 1964–1965, and helped define the Hohokam and Mogollon cultures as distinct Southwestern traditions.

personas/melvin-fowler/resumen.texto: Archaeologist at the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee who excavated Cahokia’s Mound 72 between 1967 and 1971, with its burial on a bed of shell beads and its pits of sacrificed people, and who devoted his career to the map and chronology of Cahokia.

personas/timothy-pauketat/resumen.texto: Archaeologist at the University of Illinois, a specialist in Cahokia, who holds that the city emerged suddenly around 1050 as the political and religious center of thousands of inhabitants, with regional influence comparable to that of an early state. Others, such as George Milner, propose a smaller population and power.

personas/christy-turner/resumen.texto: Bioanthropologist at Arizona State University, a specialist in human teeth and the peopling of the Americas, who from the late 1960s studied assemblages of human bones cut, burned and broken in the Southwest and argued that they were remains of cannibalism. With Jacqueline Turner he published Man Corn (1999), the center of a long debate.

personas/russell-thornton/resumen.texto: Cherokee sociologist and demographer at the University of California, Los Angeles, author of American Indian Holocaust and Survival (1987), where he estimates more than five million inhabitants for the continental territory of the United States in 1492 and about 250,000 around 1900.

personas/douglas-ubelaker/resumen.texto: Physical and forensic anthropologist at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, who estimated the Indigenous population north of Mexico around 1500 by adding up calculations by cultural area, at around two million people.

personas/brian-atwater/resumen.texto: Geologist at the United States Geological Survey who in 1987 showed, from sunken soils and dead forests on the Washington coast, that the Cascadia subduction zone produces great earthquakes. With Japanese colleagues he linked the last one to the tsunami that reached Japan in January 1700.

personas/william-n-fenton/resumen.texto: American anthropologist, the leading scholar of the Iroquois in the 20th century, author of The Great Law and the Longhouse (1998), a political history of the League. He criticized the thesis that the League inspired the United States Constitution.

personas/dean-snow/resumen.texto: Archaeologist at Pennsylvania State University who studied Mohawk villages and who, in The Iroquois (1994), placed the formation of the League around 1525 based on the sequence of settlements.

personas/john-lawson/resumen.texto: Englishman who arrived at Charleston in 1700. Between late that year and early 1701 he travelled some 970 km through the interior of the Carolinas, guided by Indigenous people, and noted the peoples he encountered. Surveyor General of the colony from 1708 and founder of Bath and New Bern, he published A New Voyage to Carolina in 1709. In September 1711 the Tuscarora captured him on the Neuse River and killed him, and his death preceded the Tuscarora War (1711–1715).

hechos/complejo-agricola-del-este/resume.texto: Between about 5,000 and 3,800 years ago the peoples of eastern North America independently domesticated local plants: a variety of squash, the sunflower, goosefoot and marsh elder (Iva annua), and later cultivated other seed crops, such as little barley. It is one of the few independent centers of domestication in the world; maize, which arrived from Mexico, only became the main crop of the East after the year 900.

hechos/cultura-de-poverty-point/resumen.texto: Peoples of the lower Mississippi Valley who, between about 1700 and 1100 BC, built the great center of earthworks and mounds at Poverty Point and other smaller sites, without agriculture, relying on fishing, hunting and gathering. They moved materials more than a thousand kilometers: copper from the Great Lakes, galena from Missouri and steatite from the Appalachians. Mounds had already been built in the region almost two millennia earlier, at Watson Brake.

hechos/cultura-adena/resumen.texto: Peoples of the Ohio Valley who, between about 800 BC and the beginning of our era, buried some of their dead in conical mounds that grew larger over time, with objects of copper, mica and engraved stone tablets, and who cultivated plants of the Eastern Agricultural Complex. The name comes from the Adena estate, near Chillicothe, where a mound was excavated in 1901.

hechos/cultura-hopewell/resumen.texto: A network of peoples of eastern North America, centered in southern Ohio and Illinois, who between about 100 BC and AD 500 built large geometric earthen enclosures and burial mounds. Their “interaction sphere” moved obsidian from the Rocky Mountains, copper from Lake Superior, mica from the Appalachians, and shells and shark teeth from the Gulf of Mexico, from which objects for the tombs were made. They cultivated local plants and gathered wild foods, living in scattered hamlets; the name comes from the Mordecai Hopewell farm in Ohio, excavated in 1891.

hechos/cultura-misisipiana/resumen.texto: Agricultural societies of the Mississippi Valley and the Southeast who, between about 800 and the 16th century, grew maize on a large scale and organized themselves into hierarchical chiefdoms with centers of platform mounds, plazas and temples. They waged war between chiefdoms, with walled villages and head trophies, and at some centers practiced human sacrifice. The chroniclers of Hernando de Soto’s expedition (1539–1543) described their last great chiefdoms, such as Coosa, before epidemics and wars undid them.

hechos/auge-de-cahokia/resumen.texto: Around 1050 the village of Cahokia was suddenly rebuilt according to a plan, with a great plaza and Monks Mound, and attracted immigrants from the region: according to tooth isotope analyses, nearly a third of those buried had been born elsewhere. It was the center of a religious and political power whose styles and symbols spread along the Mississippi. Timothy Pauketat considers it a city and nearly a state; George Milner and others, a chiefdom with a smaller population.

hechos/sacrificios-del-monticulo-72/resu.texto: Melvin Fowler excavated a small Cahokia mound between 1967 and 1971 with about 270 bodies: besides the “bead burial,” on some 20,000 shell beads, there was a pit with more than fifty young women laid out in rows, other pits with women, four men without heads or hands, and a group of about forty people who died violently, some perhaps buried alive, according to Fowler. Isotope analyses indicate that many of the sacrificed women ate more maize than the elite buried there. Fowler interpreted it as the funeral of a chief with his retinue; in 2016 Thomas Emerson and others showed that the central burial included women and proposed a ritual scene linked to fertility; both readings accept that mass sacrifices took place.

hechos/abandono-de-cahokia/titulo.texto: The Decline and Abandonment of Cahokia

hechos/abandono-de-cahokia/resumen.texto: From the late 12th century Cahokia surrounded its center with a wooden palisade with bastions, rebuilt several times, and its population declined until the site was empty around 1350. The causes proposed are war, droughts, floods on the Mississippi, the exhaustion of timber and soil, and internal political conflicts, with no agreement on which weighed most. The region between the Ohio and the Mississippi was left almost depopulated, which archaeologists call the “empty quadrant.”

hechos/complejo-ceremonial-del-sureste/r.texto: A set of symbols and images shared by Mississippian centers between about 1200 and 1650: warriors with hawk wings who carry severed heads, the eye in the hand, the cross in a circle, and horned serpents, engraved on shell and repoussé on copper. It was found mainly at Spiro, Etowah, and Moundville and is interpreted as an elite religious and prestige system linked to war and the world of the dead.

hechos/cacicazgo-de-coosa/resumen.texto: A large Mississippian chiefdom in northwestern Georgia and eastern Tennessee that, according to the chroniclers of the Hernando de Soto expedition, dominated a chain of towns stretching hundreds of kilometers in 1540; according to those same accounts, Soto held the chief as a hostage while crossing his lands and demanded carriers and women from him. When the Tristán de Luna expedition arrived in 1560, the chiefdom had been reduced and was at war with its former tributaries; its towns later regrouped among the Creeks. The identification of the towns named in the chronicles with archaeological sites is partly hypothetical.

hechos/saqueo-de-spiro/resumen.texto: Between 1933 and 1935, in the midst of the Depression, the Pocola Mining Company leased the site and dug tunnels into Craig Mound, where it found a burial chamber with textiles, feathers, engraved shells, and preserved copper, and sold the pieces to collectors in the United States and Europe. The scandal led Oklahoma to require excavation permits and the University of Oklahoma to study the site from 1936; much of what was looted was never recovered.

hechos/cementerio-de-norris-farms/titulo.texto: The Violent Deaths at Norris Farms

hechos/cementerio-de-norris-farms/resume.texto: In the Norris Farms 36 cemetery, of an Oneota culture village in the Illinois River valley dating to around 1300, George Milner and his colleagues found that about a third of the adults had died violently: arrow wounds, mace blows, scalping, and decapitation, on bodies that were sometimes left unburied for a time. They interpret this as the result of a continuous war of ambushes and small attacks that weighed on the life of the entire village.

hechos/matanza-de-crow-creek/resumen.texto: Around 1325 a fortified village of farmers on the Missouri River, in South Dakota, was attacked while it was rebuilding its defensive ditch, and in that ditch the remains of at least 486 people of all ages were found in 1978. Almost all the skulls bear scalping marks and many bodies were decapitated or mutilated; the skeletons show malnutrition and earlier wounds, and there are fewer young women than expected, which suggests that some were taken captive. Researchers attribute it to competition for land and food between villages in a time of drought.

hechos/cultura-ancestral-pueblo/resumen.texto: Peoples of the Colorado Plateau, in the Four Corners region, who went from hunter-gatherers with maize (the “basketmaker” stage, from the second millennium BC) to villages of semi-subterranean houses and then, between the 8th and 13th centuries, to stone and adobe pueblos with kivas. They built the great houses of Chaco and the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde and left the region around 1300; their descendants are the Hopi, the Zuni, and the pueblo peoples of New Mexico. The name “Anasazi,” of Navajo origin, was replaced by “Ancestral Puebloans” at the request of those peoples.

hechos/auge-de-chaco/resumen.texto: Between 850 and 1150 the Ancestral Puebloans built planned great houses in Chaco Canyon, using tens of thousands of beams brought from distant mountains, and a network of straight roads that linked it with part of the more than one hundred “great houses” of the region. Chaco gathered turquoise, shells, macaws, and cacao that came from Mesoamerica, as the cacao residues in cylindrical vessels from Pueblo Bonito showed in 2009. It is debated whether it was a pilgrimage center, a chiefdom, or an early state; its decline coincides with the drought of 1130–1180.

hechos/linaje-materno-de-pueblo-bonito/t.texto: The Pueblo Bonito Crypt and Its Matrilineage

hechos/linaje-materno-de-pueblo-bonito/r.texto: In Room 33 of Pueblo Bonito fourteen people were buried with thousands of turquoise beads, shells, and ritual objects, the richest burial in the Southwest. In 2017 the mitochondrial DNA of nine of them showed the same maternal lineage for about 330 years, which suggests a hereditary elite traced through the female line, like the kinship of present-day peoples. Some of the descendant peoples criticized the study for having been carried out without consulting them.

hechos/matanza-de-sacred-ridge/resumen.texto: Around 800, in an Ancestral Puebloan village near Durango (Colorado), about 35 people were beaten, dismembered, and burned, and the village was abandoned. James Potter and Jason Chuipka, who studied the remains, interpret it as violence between distinct ethnic groups; it is one of the oldest cases of mass violence in the Southwest. The site lies under the waters of Lake Nighthorse.

hechos/canibalismo-en-cowboy-wash/resume.texto: In semi-subterranean houses in southwestern Colorado, abandoned around 1150, the remains of at least seven dismembered people were found, with bones cut, boiled, and broken. In 2000 Richard Marlar and his team reported detecting human myoglobin in a coprolite left in a hearth, which would indicate the consumption of human flesh, and Brian Billman and his colleagues linked the episode to the drought and the Chaco crisis. Kurt Dongoske, Debra Martin, and T. J. Ferguson objected that the violence was clear but that cannibalism was not proven and that there were other explanations; many bioarchaeologists accept that it did occur in this case, and it is debated whether it was out of hunger, terror, or ritual.

hechos/debate-sobre-el-canibalismo-en-el.texto: The Debate over Cannibalism among the Ancestral Puebloans

Since the late 1960s Christy Turner has described sets of Southwestern human bones cut, burned, and broken to extract marrow, with the polish left by the cooking pot, identical to those of cooked animals; Tim White reached the same conclusion in 1992 with a site on the Mancos River, and in Man Corn (1999) Turner gathered dozens of cases, mostly between 900 and 1300, and proposed that cannibalism had come from Mexico as an instrument of terror. Critics accept the extreme violence and the processing of the bodies, but in some cases propose other explanations, such as the execution and destruction of the bodies of supposed witches (J. Andrew Darling, 1998), and reject a Mexican origin for lack of evidence. The Hopi and Zuni generally reject the claim that their ancestors were cannibals.

hechos/abandono-de-las-cuatro-esquinas/t.texto: The Abandonment of the Four Corners

hechos/abandono-de-las-cuatro-esquinas/r.texto: Around 1300 the Ancestral Puebloans left the entire Mesa Verde and Four Corners region, where tens of thousands of people had lived, and moved south to the Rio Grande valleys and to the lands of the Hopi, Zuni, and Acoma. It coincides with the great drought of 1276–1299, which Douglass identified in tree rings, and with a colder climate and more violence: at Castle Rock, around 1280, at least 41 people were killed in an attack. Archaeologists add the depletion of soil and game and the attraction of new religious forms from the south, such as the cult of the kachinas.

hechos/cultura-hohokam/resumen.texto: Peoples of the Sonoran Desert, in central and southern Arizona, who between about 300 and 1450 grew maize, beans, squash, and cotton with the largest network of irrigation canals in North America, hundreds of kilometers along the Salt and Gila rivers. They had ballcourts and platform mounds of Mesoamerican influence and, in their last phase, large houses such as Casa Grande. They declined around 1450 for disputed reasons (floods, droughts, conflicts); the Akimel and Tohono O'odham (Pima and Papago) are considered their descendants, and the name comes from an O'odham word that alludes to those who are no longer there.

hechos/cultura-mogollon/lugar.texto: Southern New Mexico and western Texas

hechos/cultura-mogollon/resumen.texto: Peoples of the mountains of southwestern New Mexico, southeastern Arizona, and northern Chihuahua who, between about 200 and 1450, lived in villages of semi-subterranean houses and later in pueblos. Its Mimbres branch painted white and black bowls with scenes and animals between 1000 and 1130; these were buried with the dead, their bottoms punched through. Paquimé, in Chihuahua, is related to its last phase. Emil Haury defined it in 1936 as a tradition distinct from that of the Ancestral Puebloans.

hechos/cultura-fremont/resumen.texto: Peoples of Utah and neighboring areas who, between the beginning of the Common Era and around 1300, combined maize cultivation with hunting and gathering. They are known for their clay figurines and for their rock art of trapezoidal human figures with ornaments. Their disappearance coincides with the arrival of Numic-speaking peoples, such as the Shoshones, Utes, and Paiutes, although the relationship between the two is debated.

hechos/dendrocronologia-del-suroeste/tit.texto: Tree Rings Date the Ruins of the Southwest

hechos/dendrocronologia-del-suroeste/res.texto: In June 1929, during an excavation at Show Low (Arizona), the charred beam HH-39 turned up; it linked the sequence of rings from living trees with that of the beams in the ruins. With it A. E. Douglass assigned calendar years to the construction of Pueblo Bonito, Mesa Verde, and dozens of other sites, and identified the great drought of 1276–1299.

hechos/expolio-y-proteccion-de-mesa-verd.texto: From the Wetherills to the Antiquities Act

In December 1888 the ranchers Richard Wetherill and Charlie Mason reached Cliff Palace; with their families they excavated the houses of Mesa Verde and sold collections to museums and private buyers, and in 1891 Gustaf Nordenskiöld sent hundreds of objects to Europe. The alarm over the looting of Mesa Verde and Chaco led to the Antiquities Act and the creation of Mesa Verde National Park, both in June 1906.

hechos/pueblos-pueblo/resumen.texto: Farming peoples of the Rio Grande valley, western New Mexico, and northeastern Arizona, descendants of the Ancestral Puebloans, who around 1540 lived in some seventy to one hundred settlements of multistory houses. They spoke languages of four different families (Tanoan, Keresan, Zuni, and Hopi) and shared irrigated maize, kivas, kachinas, and government by religious societies. The Spanish called them “pueblos” for their settlements; Coronado met them in 1540 and Juan de Oñate subjugated them from 1598.

hechos/pueblo-hopi/resumen.texto: A Uto-Aztecan-speaking pueblo on the mesas of northeastern Arizona, with villages such as Oraibi, inhabited since before 1150. Its life revolves around maize cultivation in the desert and a cycle of ceremonies with the kachinas, organized by clans and societies. Franciscan missions arrived in 1629; after the Revolt of 1680 the Hopi never again accepted Spanish rule, and in 1700 they destroyed their own town of Awatovi for having received the friars again.

hechos/destruccion-de-awatovi/resumen.texto: In late 1700, after Awatovi had again received the Franciscans, men from Oraibi and other Hopi villages attacked it, killed most of the men, burned the town, and carried off women and children. It is recounted in Hopi oral tradition and in Spanish accounts from the following years; according to tradition, some of the captives were killed on the way, and in 1964 a pit with about thirty people whose bones were cut and burned was found at Polacca Wash, which Christy Turner and Nancy Morris linked to that episode. Hopi versions differ on the causes, which include internal conflicts and accusations of witchcraft.

hechos/pueblo-navajo/resumen.texto: An Athabaskan-speaking people, related to languages of Alaska and western Canada, who arrived in the Southwest from the north between the 14th and 16th centuries; their earliest secure sites, in Dinétah in northwestern New Mexico, date to about 1500. They took farming, weaving, and religious elements from the Pueblo peoples, and sheep and horses from the Spanish. They raided pueblos and colonies to steal livestock and take captives, and at the same time they suffered Spanish and Mexican expeditions that captured Navajos to sell them as servants.

hechos/pueblos-apaches/lugar.texto: Southern New Mexico and western Texas

hechos/pueblos-apaches/resumen.texto: Athabaskan-speaking peoples of the southern Plains and the Southwest, related to the Navajos, who arrived from the north between the 14th and 16th centuries. The “Querechos” that Coronado encountered on the Plains in 1541, bison hunters who carried their belongings on dogs, were probably Apaches. Divided into independent bands (Chiricahua, Mescalero, Jicarilla, Lipan, and others), they lived by hunting, gathering, some farming and, from the 17th century, by raids on pueblos and colonies; in the 18th century the Comanches pushed them south. In turn, Spanish colonists and soldiers captured Apaches to sell them as servants, and by the late 18th century prisoners were deported in chains to Mexico and Cuba.

hechos/confederacion-iroquesa/resumen.texto: A confederacy of five Iroquoian-speaking nations of present-day New York State (Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca), to which the Tuscarora joined around 1722. According to tradition, it was founded by Deganawida and Hiawatha to end the wars and vendettas among them, with a Grand Council of fifty chiefs chosen by the clan mothers, which decided by consensus. The date is disputed: Barbara Mann and Jerry Fields proposed 1142, based on a solar eclipse; others point to the eclipse of 1451; and most archaeologists, such as Dean Snow, place it between 1450 and 1600 based on the sequence of villages. Internal peace did not prevent the League from waging war on its neighbors, especially in the 17th century.

hechos/guerras-de-duelo/titulo.texto: The Mourning Wars of the Iroquois

hechos/guerras-de-duelo/resumen.texto: Among the Iroquois and their neighbors, such as the Wendat, the death of a relative obliged vengeance or replacement with a captive, and clan mothers could call for raids to take them. Captives were adopted by the family or, according to Jesuit accounts of the 17th century, tortured in public for hours or days, executed and, in some cases, partly eaten in a rite. Daniel Richter argues that the epidemics of the 1630s and 1640s multiplied these wars, which mixed with competition for furs in the Beaver Wars.

hechos/iroqueses-del-san-lorenzo/titulo.texto: The Disappearance of the St. Lawrence Iroquoians

hechos/iroqueses-del-san-lorenzo/resumen.texto: Jacques Cartier found Iroquoian-speaking villages on the banks of the St. Lawrence River in 1535, such as Stadacona, where Quebec City now stands, and Hochelaga, where Montreal is, with longhouses, palisades, and maize fields. When Samuel de Champlain traveled the river in 1603 they no longer existed. Pottery of their style found in Wendat and Mohawk villages suggests that they were destroyed or absorbed in wars with those peoples; European epidemics and climate change are other explanations under discussion.

hechos/pueblo-wendat/resumen.texto: A confederacy of four or five Iroquoian-speaking nations living between Georgian Bay and Lake Simcoe (Ontario), in villages of longhouses with palisades, which at the beginning of the 17th century numbered between 20,000 and 30,000 people according to estimates. Maize farmers and large-scale traders, they were allies of the French and welcomed the Jesuits, who built the Sainte-Marie mission among them (1639) and studied their language; the epidemics of 1634–1640 killed nearly half of them, and in 1649 Iroquois attacks dispersed them. Their descendants are the Huron-Wendat of Wendake (Quebec) and the Wyandot of Oklahoma, Kansas, and Michigan.

hechos/pueblo-lenape/resumen.texto: Algonquian-speaking peoples of the Delaware River valley, New York Bay, and present-day New Jersey, organized in autonomous villages and in clans inherited through the female line. In the 17th century they dealt with the Dutch, Swedes, and English, among them William Penn, and in the 18th century they were pushed west, until they reached Oklahoma and Ontario. The Walam Olum, which was presented as their ancient chronicle, is an invention of Rafinesque.

hechos/confederacion-powhatan/resumen.texto: A group of some thirty Algonquian-speaking communities in eastern Virginia that paid tribute to Wahunsenacawh, the Powhatan, who had inherited six of them and added the rest through alliances and force. William Strachey wrote in 1612 that shortly before 1607 Powhatan had exterminated the Chesapeake following a prophecy; estimates of his population range from about 13,000 to 20,000 people. It was the power the English of Jamestown encountered in 1607.

hechos/tesis-de-la-influencia-iroquesa/t.texto: The Thesis of Iroquois Influence on the Constitution of the United States

hechos/tesis-de-la-influencia-iroquesa/r.texto: Donald Grinde (1977) and Bruce Johansen (1982) argued that the Iroquois League had influenced the formation of the United States and its Constitution, and in 1988 Congress passed a resolution recognizing that contribution. The documents show real contacts: the Onondaga chief Canasatego advised the colonies to unite at the Treaty of Lancaster in 1744, and Benjamin Franklin mentioned the Six Nations in 1751 when defending a union of the colonies; but the records of the 1787 convention do not mention the League. Elisabeth Tooker, William Fenton, and most historians consider that this influence on the Constitution is not proven.

hechos/tratado-de-las-dos-hileras/titulo.texto: The Two Row Wampum and the Spurious Treaty of Tawagonshi

hechos/tratado-de-las-dos-hileras/resume.texto: According to Haudenosaunee tradition, in 1613 the Mohawks and the Dutch of the area of present-day Albany agreed to live in peace like two ships sailing side by side without interfering with each other, an agreement recalled by a wampum belt with two purple rows on a white background. A document in Dutch that was presented as the written text of that treaty was declared a forgery by Charles Gehring, William Starna, and William Fenton in 1987. The wampum tradition and its use in later diplomacy do not depend on that paper, but the date of 1613 has no documentary confirmation.

hechos/revelacion-de-handsome-lake/resum.texto: In June 1799, on the lands of the chief Cornplanter, in Pennsylvania, the Seneca Handsome Lake had visions of messengers of the Creator and began to preach the Gaiwiio against alcohol, witchcraft, and the breakdown of the family, in a society battered by defeat, the loss of land, and life on reservations, where Quaker missionaries had been teaching plowing and spinning since 1798. His movement gave rise to the Longhouse religion; in its early years it also led to accusations and executions of supposed witches.

hechos/pueblo-ojibwe/resumen.texto: An Algonquian-speaking people of the Great Lakes region who, according to their tradition, traveled from the Atlantic coast to Lake Superior following a sacred shell, with a major center on Madeline Island. They kept religious knowledge on birch-bark scrolls with pictographs, used by the Midewiwin society. In the 18th and 19th centuries they expanded west in war with the Dakota, whom they displaced from much of Minnesota.

hechos/pueblo-cheroqui/resumen.texto: An Iroquoian-speaking people of the southern Appalachians, with dozens of towns grouped in regions, each with its council house, and clans inherited through the female line; Kituwah is considered their mother town. James Mooney estimated about 22,000 Cherokee around 1650. In the 18th century they sold furs and Indigenous captives to the English of Carolina and suffered great smallpox epidemics, such as that of 1738, which, according to James Adair, killed nearly half of them.

hechos/pueblo-muscogee/resumen.texto: A confederacy of Muscogee-speaking and other peoples of present-day Alabama and Georgia, formed largely by heirs of Mississippian chiefdoms such as Coosa, who regrouped after the epidemics and wars of the 16th century. Each town (talwa) had its square and council house, and the towns were divided into “white” towns of peace and “red” towns of war; their great annual festival was the Green Corn ceremony, which William Bartram described. The English called them Creeks after the streams along which they lived.

hechos/pueblo-choctaw/resumen.texto: A Muscogee-speaking people of central and southern present-day Mississippi, formed, according to archaeologists, by the union of groups dispersed after the collapse of the Mississippian chiefdoms; their tradition places their origin at the Nanih Waiya mound. Around 1700 they numbered between 15,000 and 20,000 maize farmers, and they were allies of the French against the Chickasaws, allies of the English, in wars fueled by the purchase of captives.

hechos/pueblo-natchez/resumen.texto: A people of the lower Mississippi who retained, until the 18th century, a Mississippian-type organization: a sacred ruler, the Great Sun, a hereditary nobility, and a temple with a perpetual fire on a mound. The French described a society divided into Suns, nobles, honored people, and commoners, in which nobles had to marry commoners, a rule whose functioning is debated. After their uprising of 1729, in which they killed some 230 French settlers at Fort Rosalie, the war of 1730–1731 destroyed their nation: hundreds of prisoners, among them the Great Sun, were sold as slaves in the French colony of Saint-Domingue (Haiti), and the rest took refuge among the Chickasaws and the Creeks.

hechos/funeral-de-serpiente-tatuada/titu.texto: The Funeral of the Tattooed Serpent

hechos/funeral-de-serpiente-tatuada/resu.texto: In 1725 the Tattooed Serpent, war chief of the Natchez and brother of the Great Sun, died. Antoine-Simon Le Page du Pratz, who was present, described how his two wives and several servants and attendants were strangled during the funeral to accompany him, and how the French convinced the Great Sun not to kill himself to follow his brother. It is one of the best-described funerary sacrifices in the Southeast, comparable to those that archaeology found in Mound 72 at Cahokia.

hechos/pueblo-timucua/resumen.texto: Timucuan-speaking peoples, of a language isolate, of northern Florida and southeastern Georgia, organized in chiefdoms that waged war on one another; they were maize farmers, fishers, and gatherers. The drawings of Jacques Le Moyne from the French colony of 1564, engraved by Theodor de Bry in 1591, show them, though with many European elements. From 1587 the Franciscans gathered them into missions, the government of St. Augustine demanded workers from them in rotation (repartimiento), and Fray Francisco Pareja published catechisms and a Timucua grammar between 1612 and 1627. Estimates for 1500 range from tens of thousands to some 200,000 people (Jerald Milanich); by 1700 about a thousand remained because of epidemics, wars, and slave raids by Carolina and its Indigenous allies, and the last of them left for Cuba with the Spanish in 1763.

hechos/pueblo-calusa/resumen.texto: A people of southwestern Florida who formed a hierarchical, tributary society without agriculture, sustained by fishing in the estuaries: their capital at Mound Key received tribute from dozens of towns in the southern peninsula. In 1521 they mortally wounded Juan Ponce de León; Hernando de Escalante Fontaneda, held captive among them from 1549 to 1566, recounts that they enslaved shipwrecked Spaniards and sacrificed most of them, among them his brother, and that when a chief died his servants were sacrificed. In 1566 their chief, whom the Spanish called Carlos, made a pact with Pedro Menéndez de Avilés, but the alliance broke down and Spanish soldiers killed Carlos, his successor Felipe, and several leaders before abandoning the fort and mission in 1569. Epidemics and slave raids by peoples allied with the English reduced them, and their last groups left for Cuba in the 18th century.

hechos/pueblo-caddo/resumen.texto: Caddo-speaking peoples of eastern Texas, western Louisiana, southern Arkansas, and eastern Oklahoma, heirs of mound centers such as Spiro, organized in confederacies such as the Hasinai and the Kadohadacho. Maize farmers in dispersed villages, they received in 1542 what was left of the Soto expedition, by then under Luis de Moscoso, and Spanish missionaries of the late 17th century; the name Texas comes from their word “taysha,” meaning “friend.”

hechos/difusion-del-caballo-en-las-llanu.texto: The Arrival of the Horse on the Plains

Horses brought by the Spanish to New Mexico passed to Indigenous peoples through theft and trade, especially after the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, and spread northward: the Shoshones and Comanches had them at the beginning of the 18th century, and by around 1770 almost all the peoples of the Plains used them. The horse made it possible to hunt bison and wage war at much greater distances, led farmers and gatherers to become horsemen, and changed the balance of power among peoples.

hechos/pueblo-comanche/resumen.texto: A Numic-speaking people who split from the Shoshones and moved down to the southern Plains at the beginning of the 18th century; Spanish documents from New Mexico mention them from 1706. With the horse they displaced the Apaches and dominated an enormous territory, Comancheria, from which they traded, collected tribute, and raided northern Mexico to steal livestock and take captives, whom they sold or incorporated. In 1758 they and their allies attacked the San Sabá mission in Texas, and in 1786 the governor of New Mexico, Juan Bautista de Anza, signed a peace with the chief Ecueracapa. Pekka Hämäläinen describes that power as an “empire”; its critics dispute the word, not the facts it documents.

hechos/pueblo-lakota/resumen.texto: The western branch of the “seven council fires” of the Sioux (Dakota, Nakota, and Lakota), who in the 18th century left the forests of Minnesota and, with horses and firearms, became bison hunters on the Plains. In their expansion westward they displaced the Kiowas, Crows, Cheyennes, and other peoples; according to some of their winter counts, they reached the Black Hills around 1775–1776, which they later considered their sacred land.
