Their major ceremony was the Sun Dance.

hechos/pueblo-cheyene/resumen.texto: An Algonquian-speaking people who lived as farmers in Minnesota and who in the 18th century moved to the Plains, became mounted bison hunters, and allied with the Arapahos and later with the Lakotas. They were governed by a council of forty-four peace chiefs and by military societies, and they consider the hill of Bear Butte sacred, where their prophet Sweet Medicine received their laws.

hechos/pueblos-pies-negros/resumen.texto: A confederacy of Algonquian-speaking peoples (Siksika, Kainai, and Piikani) of the northern Plains of Montana and Alberta, bison hunters who for centuries used cliffs such as Head-Smashed-In as bison jumps. In the mid-18th century they obtained horses and firearms and became the dominant power of the northwestern Plains, at war with the Shoshones, Crows, and Crees; the smallpox epidemics of 1781 and 1837 struck them hard.

hechos/pueblo-mandan/resumen.texto: A Siouan-speaking people with fortified villages of earth lodges on the Missouri River, in North Dakota; they were maize farmers and the center of a large trade among the Plains peoples and, later, with Europeans. George Catlin painted their okipa ceremony, with its ordeals of pain, in 1832. Smallpox in 1781 reduced them, and the epidemic of 1837 almost wiped them out: from some 1,600 people, barely over a hundred remained, who joined the Hidatsa and Arikara.

hechos/sacrificio-a-la-estrella-de-la-ma.texto: The Morning Star Sacrifice of the Skidi Pawnee

The Skidi Pawnees, farmers of the Nebraska plains with a religion centered on the stars, sacrificed in some years a captive girl from another people to the Morning Star: they tied her to a wooden frame and killed her with an arrow at dawn. There are American accounts from 1817, when the young Skidi warrior Petalesharo freed the victim, and from 1838, the last recorded case, in which the victim was an Oglala girl named Haxti.

hechos/epidemia-de-viruela-de-1775-1782/.texto: During the American War of Independence a smallpox epidemic swept across North America, from Boston and Mexico to the Plains, Hudson Bay, and the Pacific coast, carried by soldiers, traders, and the Indigenous trade networks themselves. Elizabeth Fenn estimates that it killed more than 130,000 people; among the peoples of the Plains and the north the mortality was enormous, and many suffered it before they had seen a European. In 1777 Washington ordered the inoculation of Continental Army recruits.

hechos/epidemia-de-viruela-de-1837/titul.texto: The 1837 Smallpox Epidemic on the Plains

hechos/epidemia-de-viruela-de-1837/resum.texto: In 1837 the steamboat St. Peter's, of the American Fur Company, carried smallpox up the Missouri River, and the disease spread among Mandans, Hidatsas, Arikaras, Blackfeet, Assiniboines, and other peoples; the Commissioner of Indian Affairs estimated in 1839 some 17,000 deaths on the upper Missouri alone. The trader Francis Chardon recorded the epidemic in his journal at Fort Clark; of some 1,600 Mandans, between one hundred and one hundred and fifty survived, according to estimates. Ward Churchill claimed from 1994 onward that the army had deliberately distributed infected blankets; in 2006 a University of Colorado committee concluded that this claim had no support in the sources he cited and called it a fabrication.

hechos/pueblo-shoshone/titulo.texto: The Shoshones and the Peoples of the Great Basin

hechos/pueblo-shoshone/resumen.texto: Numic-speaking peoples (Shoshones, Paiutes, and Utes) who, according to the most widely accepted hypothesis, spread across the Great Basin from around the year 1000; they were hunters and gatherers of pine nuts, seeds, and roots in a desert that did not allow large villages. The northern and eastern Shoshones became horsemen at the beginning of the 18th century, and the Comanches separated from them. The Shoshone woman Sacagawea accompanied the Lewis and Clark expedition (1805).

hechos/pueblo-nez-perce/titulo.texto: The Nez Perce (Nimiipuu) and the Plateau Peoples

hechos/pueblo-nez-perce/resumen.texto: Sahaptin- and Salish-speaking peoples of the Columbia Plateau, between the Rockies and the Cascade Range, who lived by salmon fishing, by roots such as camas, and by hunting, and who gathered to trade at Celilo Falls. The Nimiipuu, whom the French called Nez Perce, raised horses from the 18th century and helped the Lewis and Clark expedition in 1805; in 1877 their war with the United States ended in their surrender.

hechos/pueblo-chumash/resumen.texto: A people of the Santa Barbara coast and the Channel Islands, in California: fishers, marine mammal hunters, and acorn gatherers who lived in large permanent villages without agriculture. They built plank canoes sewn together (tomol) to cross to the islands, used shell beads as money, and painted caves with colored figures. They numbered between 10,000 and 20,000 people according to estimates when the Franciscan missions arrived, from 1772.

hechos/pueblo-pomo/resumen.texto: Peoples of seven related languages of northern California, around Clear Lake and on the coast north of San Francisco: acorn gatherers and fishers in small autonomous communities. They are known for their baskets, among the finest in the world, sometimes covered with feathers, and for using shell beads as money. In 1850, after Pomos held in servitude killed the settlers Andrew Kelsey and Charles Stone, American soldiers killed on Bloody Island, in Clear Lake, a number of Pomos that estimates place between about sixty and several hundred, many of them women and children.

hechos/pueblo-chinook/resumen.texto: Peoples of the lower Columbia River who lived by salmon and controlled the trade between the coast and the interior, in which the Chinook Jargon, a trade language that European traders later adopted, was used. They had nobles, commoners, and slaves, whom they bought and sold, and they flattened the heads of free children as a sign of rank, something forbidden to slaves. Fever epidemics of 1830–1833 killed most of them.

hechos/pueblo-haida/resumen.texto: A people of Haida Gwaii and southern Alaska, organized in two moieties (Raven and Eagle) and in lineages through the female line, known for their carved cedar poles, plank houses, and great canoes. With them they conducted war expeditions and slave raids along the coast as far as Puget Sound. The smallpox epidemic of 1862, which spread along the coast when the authorities of Victoria expelled from the city the camps of the northern peoples, reduced their population from several thousand to a few hundred by the end of the century.

hechos/pueblo-tlingit/resumen.texto: A people of the coast and islands of southeastern Alaska, organized in moieties and clans through the female line, traders between the coast and the interior and owners of slaves obtained in war. At their funerary potlatches slaves were sometimes killed or freed. They resisted the Russians, whom they expelled from Sitka in 1802, although the Russians retook it in 1804.

hechos/pueblo-kwakwakawakw/resumen.texto: Kwak'wala-speaking peoples of northern Vancouver Island and the adjacent coast, organized in lineages (numaym) with hereditary ranks, whom Franz Boas and George Hunt studied from 1886. Their potlatches, in which chiefs validated titles by distributing and sometimes destroying goods, grew in the 19th century with the wealth of the trade and the decline of the population. Their hamat'sa society represented a tamed “cannibal” in winter ceremonies; accounts of ancient cases of actual consumption of human flesh in those rites are disputed.

hechos/esclavitud-en-la-costa-noroeste/r.texto: From Alaska to northern California, the peoples of the Northwest Coast held hereditary slaves, captured in wars and raids or purchased, who worked in fishing and in the household and could be sold, given away, or killed, for example at potlatches or when a chief's house was raised. Leland Donald, drawing on testimonies from the 18th and 19th centuries, concluded that they were an important part of the population of many groups and that the institution existed before the arrival of Europeans; Kenneth Ames and Herbert Maschner show in the archaeological record the warfare and inequality of the region from much earlier. The fur trade temporarily increased the wealth of chiefs and the demand for slaves; slavery disappeared in the second half of the 19th century under pressure from Canada and the United States.

hechos/potlatch/resumen.texto: A feast of the Northwest Coast peoples in which a chief and his lineage, before guests who acted as witnesses, validated names, titles, and rights by distributing food, blankets, and other goods, which created obligations of return. In the 19th century, with the fur trade and the blankets of the Hudson's Bay Company, the potlatches of the Kwakwaka'wakw became competitions of prestige with the destruction of goods and of “coppers.” Boas described it and Marcel Mauss analyzed it in Essay on the Gift (1925).

hechos/prohibicion-del-potlatch/resumen.texto: From January 1, 1885, Canada's Indian Act punished the potlatch with imprisonment, at the request of missionaries and agents who saw it as a waste contrary to work and to “civilization”; many peoples continued to hold it in secret. In 1921 the police arrested dozens of attendees at the potlatch of the chief Dan Cranmer, twenty of them went to prison, and hundreds of masks and ceremonial objects were confiscated, which passed to museums and collectors. The ban was lifted in 1951, and part of the objects returned in 1979 and 1980 to the Kwakwaka'wakw cultural centers of Cape Mudge and Alert Bay (U'mista).

hechos/terremoto-de-cascadia-de-1700/res.texto: On January 26, 1700, around nine o'clock at night, an earthquake of magnitude close to 9 on the Cascadia subduction zone sank the coast from Vancouver Island to northern California and caused a tsunami that reached Japan, where it was recorded. Brian Atwater showed the sunken soils and dead forests of the coast in 1987, and in 1996 Kenji Satake and his colleagues dated the earthquake using Japanese documents. The oral traditions of coastal peoples, such as the Huu-ay-aht and the Makah, speak of a great shaking and a flood that destroyed villages.

hechos/excavacion-de-ozette/resumen.texto: In 1970, after waves uncovered the remains of houses, the archaeologist Richard Daugherty, of Washington State University, began to excavate with the Makah tribe the village of Ozette, buried by a mudslide around 1700–1750. Over eleven years more than 55,000 wooden, fiber, and bone objects were recovered, from whaling harpoons to baskets and games, which are held by the Makah Cultural and Research Center, opened in 1979 at Neah Bay.

hechos/mito-de-los-constructores-de-mont.texto: During the 19th century many Americans held that the mounds and earthworks of the East had been built by a lost and more civilized race (Israelites, Welsh, Toltecs, Vikings, or Atlanteans were proposed), later exterminated by the Indians, who were considered incapable of such works. It was spread by antiquarians such as Caleb Atwater (1820) and Josiah Priest (1833) and sustained by Squier and Davis (1848), and, according to historians such as Robert Silverberg (1968), it served to present the Indians as intruders at the time of their expulsion to the west. Thomas Jefferson had already excavated a mound as an Indian grave, and Cyrus Thomas's 1894 report demonstrated that the mounds had been raised by the ancestors of the Indigenous peoples. From this belief came frauds such as the Bat Creek stone, the Davenport tablets (1877), and the “Michigan relics.”

hechos/excavacion-de-jefferson/titulo.texto: Jefferson's Excavation of a Virginia Mound

hechos/excavacion-de-jefferson/resumen.texto: Thomas Jefferson had a trench dug through a burial mound near the Rivanna River, in Virginia, to find out who had built it and for what purpose. He observed superimposed layers of bones and earth, estimated that it contained about a thousand skeletons of all ages, and concluded that it was a communal grave of the Indians, with no signs of battle. He published this in his Notes on the State of Virginia (1785); it is considered one of the first excavations to record the strata.

hechos/relevamiento-de-monticulos-de-tho.texto: The Bureau of Ethnology's Survey of Mounds

In 1881 Congress gave funds to the Smithsonian's Bureau of Ethnology to study the mounds of the East, and John Wesley Powell put Cyrus Thomas in charge in 1882. His agents visited thousands of sites in more than twenty states, excavated hundreds of mounds, and collected tens of thousands of objects; the 1894 report concluded that they had been built by various Indigenous peoples, some of them still in the period of contact. One of the pieces he then accepted as authentic, the Bat Creek stone, turned out to be a fraud.

hechos/fraude-del-walam-olum/resumen.texto: In 1836 Constantine Rafinesque published the Walam Olum, which he presented as a pictographic chronicle of the Lenape copied from wooden tablets that no one else had seen; it recounted the creation of the world and a long migration from Asia. In 1954 a study financed by Eli Lilly and published in Indiana treated it as authentic, and it circulated as Lenape history. Linguists already doubted its language, and in 1994 David Oestreicher showed, using Rafinesque's drafts, that the Lenape text had been translated from English: it is a 19th-century invention.

hechos/piedra-de-bat-creek/resumen.texto: In February 1889 John Emmert, an agent of the mound survey, said he had found in a Tennessee mound a stone with an inscription that Cyrus Thomas published as Cherokee script. In 1971 Cyrus Gordon read it as ancient Hebrew and presented it as evidence of a voyage of Hebrews to America; in 2004 Robert Mainfort and Mary Kwas showed that the inscription copies an illustration from a Masonic book of 1870, so they consider it a fraud, probably by Emmert himself.

hechos/poblacion-de-norteamerica-antes-d.texto: How Many People: The Population North of Mexico around 1500

Estimates of the population of present-day United States and Canada around 1500 range from about one million to eighteen million: James Mooney (1928) calculated some 1.15 million and Alfred Kroeber (1939) about 900,000; Henry Dobyns (1983) reached 18 million assuming early and massive epidemics; Douglas Ubelaker (1988), adding cultural areas, about 1.9 million; William Denevan (1992), about 3.8 million, and Russell Thornton (1987), more than 7 million. Reliable documentary counts begin in the 18th century, and the 1900 United States census recorded some 237,000 Indigenous people. Critics of the high figures, such as David Henige, object that they assume epidemics that left no record; critics of the low ones, such as Dobyns and Thornton, started from populations already reduced by epidemics. The distance between the two sides remains unresolved.

hechos/cultura-tchefuncte/resumen.texto: A hunter-gatherer culture of the lower Mississippi and the Gulf Coast, defined at its eponymous site, a clam-shell midden on Lake Pontchartrain in Louisiana. It is dated from 600 BC to AD 200, although some accounts have it beginning around 1000 BC. It succeeded Poverty Point, from whose exchange network it preserved much less, and it was the first in Louisiana to make pottery in large quantities, with footed vessels found from eastern Texas to eastern Florida. Its successor was the Marksville culture.

hechos/arcaico-de-norteamerica/resumen.texto: A period of about 8000 to 1000 BC that follows the Clovis and Folsom hunters and is characterized by a subsistence economy based on nuts, seeds and shellfish. It includes, among others, the Watson Brake mounds in Louisiana, around 3500 BC; the Windover pond cemetery in Florida, with at least 168 individuals dating from between 8,000 and 7,000 years ago, whose DNA was sequenced from brain tissue; and the Old Copper culture of the Great Lakes, with objects dated between 6500 and 1580 BC depending on the site.

lugares/windover/resumen.texto: An Archaic cemetery in a Florida peat bog, used about 7,000 to 8,000 years ago, with more than 160 bodies preserved in the mud along with plant-fiber textiles and remains of brain tissue. It shows hunter-gatherers who cared for the sick and the disabled for years.

lugares/koster/resumen.texto: A site in the Illinois River valley with about twenty superimposed occupation layers, from about 9,000 years ago to the 13th century, which made it possible to trace the shift from hunter camps to stable villages. It has some of the oldest dog burials in the Americas.

lugares/watson-brake/resumen.texto: A ring of eleven earthen mounds joined by embankments, about 280 meters in diameter, in northern Louisiana, built about 5,400 to 5,000 years ago by hunters, fishers, and gatherers. It is the oldest dated mound complex in North America.

lugares/poverty-point/resumen.texto: A major ceremonial center in northern Louisiana, with six concentric C-shaped embankments and several mounds, among them Mound A, one of the largest in North America. It was built by hunters, fishers, and gatherers without agriculture, who brought copper from the Great Lakes and stone from the Appalachians; it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2014.

lugares/grave-creek-mound/resumen.texto: A conical burial mound of the Adena culture, about 19 meters high, in Moundsville (West Virginia), one of the largest of its type. Its owners dug tunnels into it in 1838, finding two tombs and a stone with a supposed inscription that fueled theories of Old World visitors for a century.

lugares/serpent-mound/resumen.texto: A mound in the shape of an undulating serpent, 411 meters long, in southern Ohio: the largest known serpent effigy. Its date is disputed: a 1996 study attributed it to the Fort Ancient culture, around 1070, and a 2014 study to the Adena culture, around 300 BC. Frederic Ward Putnam bought it in 1887 to save it, one of the first acts of archaeological preservation in the United States.

lugares/newark-earthworks/resumen.texto: The largest complex of geometric earthen enclosures of the Hopewell culture, in Ohio, with a large circle and an octagon joined to another circle, surveyed by Squier and Davis in 1848. In 1982 astronomers Ray Hively and Robert Horn showed that the octagon is aligned with the extremes of the 18.6-year lunar cycle; since 2023 it has been part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

lugares/mound-city/resumen.texto: A Hopewell enclosure beside the Scioto River, near Chillicothe, with some twenty burial mounds that held carved pipes with animal figures, mica, copper, and obsidian brought from far away. A World War I military camp destroyed much of the site, which was later rebuilt.

lugares/cahokia/resumen.texto: The largest city north of Mexico before the arrival of Europeans, across the river from present-day St. Louis, with some 120 mounds, large plazas, and Monks Mound, about 30 meters high. It flourished between 1050 and 1200, with a population estimated, depending on the author, at anywhere from a few thousand to 15,000 or more; it was abandoned around 1350. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1982.

lugares/aztalan/resumen.texto: A fortified village with a palisade and platform mounds in Wisconsin, related to Cahokia, occupied between 1100 and 1300. Its first visitors gave it the name Aztlán in 1836, the homeland of the Mexica, on the mistaken belief that the Mexica had come from there; cut and burned human bones led to talk of cannibalism, an interpretation that is debated.

lugares/moundville/resumen.texto: A Mississippian center in Alabama with 29 platform mounds arranged around a large plaza, the capital of a chiefdom in the Black Warrior valley between 1120 and 1450. After 1300 it became mainly a burial place for the elite; Clarence B. Moore excavated there in 1905 and 1906.

lugares/etowah/resumen.texto: A Mississippian center in northern Georgia with six mounds, the largest about 19 meters high, and elite burials with repoussé copper plates of winged warriors, found in 1884 for Cyrus Thomas's survey. Around 1540, when Hernando de Soto passed through, it depended on the Coosa chiefdom.

lugares/spiro/resumen.texto: A Caddo ceremonial center in eastern Oklahoma, the westernmost outpost of the Mississippian culture, which gathered engraved shell objects, copper, textiles, and feathers from across the region. Its Craig Mound was looted between 1933 and 1935 by a company of treasure hunters that sold thousands of pieces to collectors.

lugares/ocmulgee/resumen.texto: An early Mississippian center in present-day Macon, Georgia, with platform mounds and an earth council house with a bench for 47 people. The Creeks consider it part of their ancestral territory; William Bartram described its ruins in 1774.

lugares/mound-key/resumen.texto: An island in Estero Bay, in southwestern Florida, formed partly of shell mounds, which was the capital of the Calusa (Calos). Hernando de Escalante Fontaneda was held captive there, and in 1566 Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded there a fort and a Jesuit mission that lasted only a few years.

lugares/gran-aldea-de-los-natchez/resume.texto: The ceremonial center of the Natchez in present-day Natchez, Mississippi, with the mound of the Great Sun's house and the mound of the perpetual fire temple, described by the French in the early 18th century. The funeral of the Tattooed Serpent was held there in 1725; it was abandoned after the war with the French of 1729–1731.

lugares/sitio-de-crow-creek/resumen.texto: A fortified village on the Missouri River, in South Dakota, first occupied by ancestors of the Mandans and, from the 12th century, by Caddoan-speaking farmers related to the Arikaras. There, in 1978, the remains of at least 486 people killed in an attack around 1325 were found.

lugares/knife-river/resumen.texto: Remains of earth-lodge villages of the Hidatsas in North Dakota, a major trading center between the Missouri farmers and the peoples of the Plains. There Lewis and Clark met Sacagawea in 1804; the smallpox epidemic of 1837 decimated its inhabitants.

lugares/head-smashed-in/resumen.texto: A bison jump in Alberta, used for some 5,700 years by Plains peoples and, in recent centuries, by the Blackfoot, to hunt bison by driving them toward the edge of the cliff. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1981.

lugares/medicine-wheel-bighorn/resumen.texto: A stone circle about 25 meters in diameter with 28 spokes, at almost 3,000 meters above sea level in the Bighorn Mountains (Wyoming), a sacred site for the Crows, Shoshones, Cheyennes, and other peoples. Its date is uncertain, and the proposal of astronomer John Eddy (1974) that it marks the solstice and the rising of bright stars is disputed.

lugares/chaco-canyon/resumen.texto: A canyon in northwestern New Mexico where the Ancestral Puebloans built, between 850 and 1150, a dozen multistory stone “great houses,” linked by straight roads to dozens of communities in the region. It was a ceremonial and political center that gathered turquoise, macaws, and cacao brought from Mesoamerica; it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.

lugares/pueblo-bonito/resumen.texto: The largest of the great houses of Chaco, with a D-shaped plan, some 650 rooms up to four or five stories high, and dozens of kivas, built in stages between 850 and 1150. In its Room 33 an elite was buried for three centuries with thousands of turquoise beads.

lugares/mesa-verde/resumen.texto: A mesa in southwestern Colorado inhabited by the Ancestral Puebloans between 550 and 1300, with some 600 houses built into the cliffs in the 13th century. It was declared a national park in 1906, the first created to protect human-made works, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978.

lugares/cliff-palace/resumen.texto: The largest cliff house at Mesa Verde, with about 150 rooms and 23 kivas, inhabited by about a hundred people in the 13th century and abandoned before 1300. It was visited in 1888 by the ranchers Richard Wetherill and Charlie Mason.

lugares/canyon-de-chelly/resumen.texto: A canyon in northeastern Arizona with ruins of the Ancestral Puebloans, such as the White House, occupied by the Navajos since the 18th century and still inhabited by Navajo families. In 1805 a Spanish expedition killed more than a hundred Navajos there, according to the report of its commander, in what is known as Massacre Cave; in 1864 Kit Carson's troops destroyed their fields and orchards.

lugares/montezuma-castle/resumen.texto: A five-story house built into a cliff in Arizona by the Sinagua between the 12th and 14th centuries. Settlers named it after Montezuma, on the mistaken belief that the Aztecs had built it; it was one of the first national monuments, in 1906.

lugares/casa-grande-arizona/resumen.texto: A large four-story building of hardened earth, built by the Hohokam at the beginning of the 14th century beside the Gila River, with openings aligned with the sun and the moon. The Jesuit Eusebio Kino visited it in 1694 and gave it its name; in 1892 it became the first archaeological site protected by the government of the United States.

lugares/snaketown/resumen.texto: A large Hohokam village beside the Gila River, on land of the Gila River Indian Community, with ballcourts, mounds, and irrigation canals. It was excavated by Harold Gladwin and Emil Haury in 1934–1935 and by Haury in 1964–1965; by decision of the community it is closed to the public.

lugares/awatovi/resumen.texto: A Hopi village in northeastern Arizona, with a Franciscan mission from 1629, visited by men of Coronado in 1540. In late 1700 it was destroyed by men of other Hopi villages for having again accepted the friars; the Peabody Museum at Harvard excavated it between 1935 and 1939.

lugares/oraibi/resumen.texto: A Hopi village on the Third Mesa, founded before 1150 and considered one of the longest continuously inhabited places in the United States. In 1906 it split between supporters and opponents of the school and the government's demands, and the opponents founded Hotevilla.

lugares/taos-pueblo/resumen.texto: A Tiwa-speaking pueblo in northern New Mexico, with two large multistory adobe buildings built between the 11th and 15th centuries, continuously inhabited. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992; in 1970 the government of the United States returned to it Blue Lake, its sacred place.

lugares/acoma-pueblo/resumen.texto: A Keres-speaking pueblo built on a mesa about 110 meters high in New Mexico, inhabited since about 1150, one of the longest continuously inhabited places in the United States. In December 1598 its inhabitants killed Juan de Zaldívar and about ten Spaniards who had climbed up to ask for provisions; in January 1599 Juan de Oñate's troops took the mesa, and about 800 Acomas died according to the most-cited figures. Oñate sentenced the survivors over twelve years of age to twenty years of servitude and, in addition, the men over 25 to the loss of a foot.

lugares/ozette/resumen.texto: A whaling village of the Makah on the Olympic Peninsula (Washington), occupied for some two thousand years, where a mudslide buried several plank houses around 1700–1750. The mud preserved wood, baskets, and nets; its excavation between 1970 and 1981 recovered more than 55,000 objects.

lugares/sgang-gwaay/resumen.texto: A Haida village at the southern end of Haida Gwaii (British Columbia), with remains of plank houses and carved cedar poles, abandoned around 1880 after smallpox epidemics. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1981.

lugares/cataratas-de-celilo/resumen.texto: Rapids on the Columbia River where the peoples of the Plateau and the lower Columbia fished for salmon and traded for some ten thousand years, one of the largest Indigenous markets in North America. They were submerged in 1957, when The Dalles Dam closed.
